summary: This document extends STAMP to measure performance on every member link of a Link Aggregation Group. Knowing each link's metrics lets operators steer traffic across member links based on performance.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road has several lanes, you test the speed of each lane to send cars to the fastest. This does so for bundled network links.

questions: what is the micro-session id tlv
how does stamp measure lag member links
subtitle: A STAMP extension that lets each member link of a bundled connection be measured and validated separately.

tldr.problem: A STAMP test session over a Link Aggregation Group cannot, by itself, measure the performance of every physical member link. Operators need per-link numbers to steer traffic by delay and loss.
tldr.mechanism: One micro STAMP session runs per member link. Test packets carry a new Micro-session ID TLV (type 11) holding the sender and reflector member link identifiers, which each side uses to validate the link a packet used.
tldr.outcome: Operators can get STAMP delay, delay variation and packet loss metrics for each member link, without adding any new state to STAMP.

today: RFC 9534 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2024. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The OWAMP and TWAMP version of this idea is in RFC 9533.

sections.title: Why Measure Each Member Link
sections.content:
A Link Aggregation Group (LAG) combines several physical links into one logical link, giving more bandwidth and better resiliency. Traffic is usually spread over the members by a hash-based mechanism, and the delay may differ between members, especially in a wide area network. Steering time-sensitive traffic by link delay and loss therefore requires measuring each member link, and the results can work together with RFC 8668 attributes.

STAMP (RFC 8762) is an active measurement method that measures both one-way and round-trip metrics such as delay, delay variation and packet loss. A STAMP session over a LAG can use a specially constructed 5-tuple to measure one member link. Without knowledge of each member link, though, it cannot measure every physical member link. This document extends STAMP to do that, giving the same metrics as OWAMP (RFC 4656) and TWAMP (RFC 5357).
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle of links is like a road with several lanes. We want to time each lane on its own, not just the whole road.

sections.title: Micro Sessions on a LAG
sections.content:
The RFC covers a LAG that directly connects two nodes. One session per member link is established between the two endpoints, and these are called micro sessions. They are ordinary STAMP sessions on member links whose test packets MUST carry member link information for validation.

All micro sessions of a LAG share the same Sender IP Address and Receiver IP Address. They may share one Sender Port and Receiver Port pair or each use its own; the shared pair is simpler to operate and is RECOMMENDED. A micro STAMP Session-Sender MAY also include the Follow-Up Telemetry TLV from RFC 8972 to request information from the Reflector. The RFC says this timestamp can improve delay accuracy by minimizing the impact of egress queuing delays.
sections.plainLanguage: We run one small test in each lane. All the tests start and end at the same two places.

sections.title: The Micro-session ID TLV
sections.content:
The STAMP TLV mechanism of RFC 8972 lets optional TLVs extend STAMP test packets. This RFC defines the Micro-session ID TLV with Type value 11. Besides the STAMP TLV Flags, Type and Length, it holds two 2-octet fields: the Sender Micro-session ID and the Reflector Micro-session ID.

The Length field MUST be 4, the number of octets in the Value. The sender and reflector identifiers each carry the LAG member link identifier for that side, and each MUST be unique within a STAMP session at the Session-Sender or Session-Reflector respectively. The RFC notes they could later be used beyond LAGs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test packet carries a small tag naming the sender's lane and the reflector's lane.

sections.title: Micro STAMP Test Procedures
sections.content:
Micro STAMP-Test reuses the procedures of RFC 8762. The Session-Sender MUST send test packets over the member link its session is associated with. The mapping between a micro session and the member link identifiers can be configured by augmenting the STAMP YANG model, but that augmentation is out of scope here.

The Sender MUST set the Sender Micro-session ID. It MUST set the Reflector Micro-session ID if it knows it, and otherwise leaves it zero. The Reflector identifier can be preconfigured or learned from the data plane, such as from the reflected packet, and the RFC does not specify how.

If the Reflector Micro-session ID is not zero, the Reflector checks it against its own session and MUST discard the packet if the check fails. A zero value is not verified. On success it reflects the packet with both identifiers filled in, copying the Sender identifier from the received packet. The Sender then validates the Sender Micro-session ID against the expected member link and the Reflector Micro-session ID to check the Reflector's behavior, discarding the packet on any failure.

Micro STAMP supports both stateless and stateful Reflector modes. It adds no state to STAMP, so any procedure involving the Micro-session ID is stateless.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides check each other's lane tag. A packet with a wrong tag is thrown away, and checking a tag does not require remembering anything extra.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has allocated value 11 in the STAMP TLV Types registry for the Micro-session ID TLV, referencing this document. That is the same value the TLV format uses in its Type field.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of STAMP tag types now has a new entry, number 11, for the lane tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is meant for the LAG case where the Session-Sender and Session-Reflector are directly connected. The RFC assumes a node in a STAMP operation has already verified the integrity of the LAG connection and the identity of its one-hop-away peer.

It introduces no additional security issues, and the security mechanisms of RFC 8762 and RFC 8972 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends are directly connected and already trust each other, so the older STAMP safety rules are enough.

fields.name: STAMP TLV Flags
fields.desc: Flags field of the STAMP TLV.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Set to 11 for the Micro-session ID TLV.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the Value field in octets; MUST be 4.

fields.name: Sender Micro-session ID
fields.desc: LAG member link identifier of the sender side.

fields.name: Reflector Micro-session ID
fields.desc: LAG member link identifier of the reflector side.
